issues.legal_issue: A trial court must not reject both parties’ accounts and substitute a factual account of its own, but the evidence may still support conviction if the appellate court finds the prosecution account established.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the parties’ accounts of how the incident began and formulated its own version.
The Supreme Court agreed that the trial court was not justified in making out a case of its own.
On its own assessment of the evidence, the Supreme Court found the prosecution account of the incident credible and supported by other evidence.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s approach to the competing accounts was erroneous, but the Supreme Court accepted the prosecution version on the evidence and did not set aside the convictions on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A court must sift the evidence rather than invent a third version after rejecting the accounts presented by the parties. The judgment cites no earlier cases or statutory provisions for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.trial_court_rejected_both_accounts: The trial court rejected the accounts of the incident advanced by both the prosecution and the defence.
predicates.trial_court_created_own_account: The trial court formulated its own account of how the incident occurred.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal concerns a trial court that rejected both parties’ accounts and formulated its own, the rule requires the factfinder not to substitute an unproved third version.

issues.legal_issue: A person in possession of property may exercise private defence against an entry on that property only when the entry amounts to an offence, and an attacker who launches a murderous assault cannot rely on private defence against the victims’ response.
material_facts: The complainant party entered land in the accused party’s possession to ask them to withdraw, claiming ownership and possession.
The evidence did not establish that the complainant party entered with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the persons in possession.
The accused party launched a murderous attack, causing three deaths and serious injuries; the attack was prepared in advance.
issues.conclusion: The accused had no right of private defence of property because the entry was not criminal trespass, and the murderous attack disentitled them from claiming private defence of person.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 96, 97 and 99 of the Indian Penal Code govern the existence and restrictions of private defence; Section 97 permits defence of property against specified offences. Under Section 441, unauthorised entry constitutes criminal trespass only if accompanied by the specified intent. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this principle.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_involving_private_de: The proceeding is a criminal case in which an accused claims private defence of person or property.
predicates.unauthorised_entry_without_prohibited_in: A person entered property without authority to persuade those in possession to withdraw, and did not enter with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy them.
predicates.accused_launched_murderous_attack: The accused initiated a murderous assault on the persons who entered the property.

issues.definition: If a private-defence claim arises after an unauthorised but non-criminally intended entry and the accused launch a murderous attack, the rule means the accused have no right to private defence.

issues.legal_issue: The exception for causing death while exercising private defence does not reduce a murder conviction when the attack is premeditated and intended to cause more harm than necessary, even if the other party committed criminal trespass.
material_facts: The accused party had gone to the land determined to cultivate it and prepared to resist any interference.
The attack caused numerous severe injuries and three deaths, while the accused party’s injuries were comparatively minor.
The Supreme Court held that the attack was premeditated and intended to cause more harm than necessary for private defence.
issues.conclusion: Even if the complainant party had committed criminal trespass, the murder convictions would not be disturbed under Exception 2 to Section 300; the exception did not apply to this premeditated, excessive attack.
issues.legal_principle: Section 104 of the Indian Penal Code limits private defence against criminal trespass by excluding the voluntary causing of death. Exception 2 to Section 300 does not apply where the attack is premeditated and intended to cause more harm than necessary for private defence. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this conclusion.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_murder_conviction and criminal_trespass_by_other_party and premeditated_attack and intended_excessive_harm

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_murder_convictio: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a murder conviction.
predicates.criminal_trespass_by_other_party: The other party entered or remained on property with the intent that makes the conduct criminal trespass.
predicates.premeditated_attack: The accused prepared for and launched the attack with prior determination.
predicates.intended_excessive_harm: The accused intended to cause more harm than was necessary to defend person or property.

issues.definition: If a murder appeal involves criminal trespass by the other party and a premeditated attack intended to cause excessive harm, the rule means the murder conviction is not reduced under the private-defence exception.

issues.legal_issue: A court may accept evidence against some accused while acquitting others, because the maxim that false evidence in one respect must be rejected entirely does not apply in criminal trials.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted ten accused but convicted the appellants after considering the case of each accused separately.
The Supreme Court found the eyewitness evidence cogent, consistent, and corroborated by medical and other evidence.
The reasons supporting the acquittals were not applicable to the appellants whose participation the evidence established.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals of other accused did not require the appellants’ acquittal; the convictions of the appellants were upheld on the evidence assessed against them individually.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus does not apply in criminal trials. The court must separate truth from falsehood and assess the evidence against each accused. The judgment cites no earlier cases or statutory provisions for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.some_coaccused_were_acquitted: The trial court acquitted some persons accused in the same case.
predicates.accused_participation_individually_estab: The evidence, assessed against the particular accused, established that person’s participation.

issues.definition: If some co-accused were acquitted but the evidence individually establishes the appellant’s participation, the rule means the co-accused’s acquittal does not require the appellant’s acquittal.

issues.legal_issue: An accused whose position is the same as that of acquitted accused omitted from the initial report should also be acquitted when the trial court has acquitted those others on that basis.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted accused whose names did not appear in the initial report.
One appellant’s name also did not appear in that report.
The Supreme Court considered that appellant to stand on the same footing as the acquitted accused.
issues.conclusion: The appeal of the appellant omitted from the initial report was allowed, while the appeals of the other appellants were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court applied parity with the acquitted accused in the circumstances of this case, concluding that the appellant omitted from the initial report stood on the same footing as those acquitted. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_omitted_from_initial_report: The accused’s name was not included in the initial report of the incident.
predicates.similarly_situated_to_acquitted_accused: The accused stood on the same relevant footing as persons acquitted because their names were omitted from the initial report.

issues.definition: If an accused appealing a conviction was omitted from the initial report and stood on the same footing as acquitted accused, the rule means that accused’s appeal is allowed.
